THE WARRINGTON SCANDAL. ACTION FOR BREACH OF PROMISE. ..C2CO DAMAGES. The circumstances of a very heartless breach of promise, in which a Warrington churchwarden figured as defendant, were inquired into at a sitting of the Sheriffs Court held on Monday morning, at the Shelley Arms, Preston, before Mr. E. T. Wilson, Acting Under Sheriff. A jury had been empanelled for the puruose of assessing damages, the defendant ; having in the initiatory stages allowed judgment to go by default. The plaintiff was a young woman, 2fi years of age, named Emily Perdu, who resides I with her parents at Liverpool, and the defendant was George Samuel Holmes, 42 years of age, late of , Lovely-lane, Warrington. Mr. Tomlinson, of Pres- ton, appeared for the plaintiff, but the defendant: did not appear; neither was he represented. A ILMARTLIffNA PINCH OF orramon. tutoring the ease beforethe court, Mr. Tomlinson said j that the defendant had been served with a writ, tie had , allowed judgment to go by default, bad thereby admitted the breach, and therefore he (Mr. Tomlinson) thought the plaintiff was entitled to souse damagou in respect of that breach. In assessing the (141.111,CS the jury were entitled to take into romideration not 'only the position j plaintiff had lost, but any circumstances of aggravation, J suels as heartless deception on the part of defendant. He thought that when they had heard the circumstances , they would come to the etinclusion that the defendant had been guilty of as heartless apices' of ileception as Was ever practiced by a mats towards a woman.j , Plaintiff was an histi,l bmkkeeper, and had been I employed at the Adelphi Hotel, Liverpool, and the Great Northern Hotel, Lincoln. She left the latter place about j the end of October last year, and went to live with j 1 her parents at Liverpool until she could get another j situation. About a week afterwards she met the defendant, who paid her marked attention. Eventually, he pbsposed marriage to her and she accepted him. From that time the puns corresponded regularly in I very affectionate terms, and defendant was a regular ! visitor at the house of plaintiff's parents. He pressed for an early date to be fined bre the marriage, and saki- ' I nudely. January 31st this year was appointed Defend- , ant sail he Was a valuer fora tire he:simnel. company, and he stated that his avenge earnings amounted to between £6 and £7 per week, while occasionally he made considerably snore titan that. He had a house at War- rington and offices at Liverpool, and he occupied, as he stated, the position of churchwarden at Warrington. That appeanhl to be true, but he also said something j Which WAS nottrue, and that was that he was a widower I with one child, while, in fact, he WAS a married man, j and actually living with his wife at Warrington at the time 'risings went on until the middle of January, I when, at his request, the marriage was postponed till the I end of February. her-arise he fell ill. T. LOWNPTION 1.120A.F.0. Matters went on as before until approsching the end of February, when, defendant seeing that hr, most either give up plaintiff or commit bigamy—for he was a married man at the time—wrote kern letter intimating that on account of his different,eu with her family the marriage had better he broken off. On receiving this letter plaintiff went over to Warrington, SAW the vicar of St. Itarnalsas' parish, and from Got gentleman learned forth,. first time that Holmes was A married man. Perliiiim the most temarkalie thing about the rase was that the plaintiff had actually visited the defendant's house an.l hail Oa, prepared by his wife, and nothing WAS said by whieh the plaintiff mild tell that the defendant was a married man. Hut unfortu- nately even all he had told the jury was not the worst part of the bitsineks, fro just before the first date fined for the marriage the plaintiff had allowed herself to be seduced, and she yet hail a lot of trouble before her. The only motivrthat could be a.ignesl for the defendant's action was that he entenst upon this enterprise with the deliberate and only intention of ruining the plaintiff at whatever cost, although had to bring himself within this pale of the criminal law by committing bigamy. But unfortunately Ise hail not brought himself into tire pale of criminal law, for he effected his purpose without, but he had brought himself within the pale of the civil law. and he (Mr. Tomlinson) hoe.' the jury would take all the aggravating eircumstanes'ss of the ease into con- sideration in assessing damages tor the wrong plaintiff had suffered. PLAINTIFF IN T. WITNIESS BOX. Emily Perdu, the plaintiff, was then called. In enc. roborating the statement of her solicitor she mid she left J Use Great Northern Hotel, LineoMat the end id Onolhir, went to Liverpool, and met the defendant about a week j afterwards. He first spoke about marriage in the early nart of December, wishing it to take place early. It was fined for the 31st of January, and she bought everything, including her dress for the marriage, and invited her friend' for that slate. On the pleats( sickn.s on the part of the defendant the marriage wm postponed, and even- tually it was remnanted foetheessil of February.

In the course of further evidence the plaintiff said that ii,, the 21st February she retietved the following, letter from the defendant t—i'• My dear Ernmie,—l ant in re- ceipt ef ytour three letters, and I should have answered the first one but I have really toun awfully busy pack- ing tap my furniture for storage, and sending them away to Liverpool on Saturday. I intend leaving here, add going to Manchester. I was awfully armored last time I was itt your house at the nuttaterat if different people in your house, and I certainly have come to the con- clusion that it would be far Ixttiv that our engagement came to an end. I cannot help no feelings. but lam confident that I cannot be happy with your family. I know this may pain you, but I have refrained from writing this to one thinking that it might blow over, but no. I cannot think that we could ever be happy ' together. tarn deeply grieved for the past, but it is of no use to marry unless you tun he happy. but I feel that cannot be united to your family, and that it certainly cannot he. Trusting that you may tfleet with one more worthy of you than, yours very sincerly, IL S. Houses." Continuing, witness said that up to that time she had never heard that the defendant mass married man. She Iliad liven to his house at Warrington, and saw it woman there, whom defendant said was his bousekerper. She prepared tea for her and the defendant, and she did not enter the mom while she was Arnim with the defendant. The fimt time that Pile heerd the defendant was a married man was on the 25th February. from the vicar of St. Itarnabas•Chstrch.Warrington. Speaking of what I had taken place just previous to the first date fined for the marriage. plaintiff said shit reiviveil 0 letter in which defendant said t—'• My own darling little pet—l feel as if new that you really and truly were my own, and my Ices for you knows no bounds, ior I bine you a thousand rent. more than I have done sine,. I first saw you. I know you can trust no, and if I did tott feel that, where would our united lave he? I feel as if to be separated even for a night is too mueli for me, and I want to bP always mow you. Oil, may lioil bleat you, little Palmy, and keep you under the shadow of His heavenly wings. I know I strain your love to the highest pitch, but lean' not help it. I could write voluntes to you, but suffice it to say that no man eould pomibly have the same love for a WOMall as I have for you—With all loveand kisses I remain, your OMII toeing intended husband, G. S. Holum."

SUMMER RAMBLES ROUND MANCHESTER. _ .DUCK DECOY, lIALN. . .
The following appears M the "Manchester Guardian from the pen of Mr. Alfred Itimmer. . •

There are not many persons lit ing in Manchester I or Liverpool who would easily believe that almost within • direct line between the two cities there is a decoy for the capture of wild ducks which is in full working order and rendering abundant results. In the season that ended on the lot of March, the head keeper told me, on reference to hie books, he had captured 856 wild ducks, this of course includ- ing teal ; yet this olocoy in within sight of the Run- corn viaduct, which crosses the Mersey not much ! more than a mile away. It is in • meadow farm, and well secluded from the highroad. !fere the wonderful instincts of ducks can he seen. So well it, thee know when they are safe that a few yarffe—say the Isititelary of a pirk paling-osinverts then, from wild to almost tame ducks, and they sit as quietly in an absoletnly preserved pool as if they were on a Canadian marsh. Lancashire has ceased to have great undrained marsh.. With itt western parts expiated to the Irish Sea, theusands 4 tillCkz.l were always to be seen on Martin or I lettere Metes, near Ormskiik. But ducks hove a strange hankering after their old localitim. They still are abundant in England, and that to an extent that few would credit. 1 aaw myself on the pond in the Hale decoy no lese than 300 ducks, including teal. The construction of the deer I will endeavour to describe, and also the manner In which the fowl are captured. Hale Decoy is a five-sided enclosure, and it to surrounded by a broad moat, which can only be cumeed at one part, where there itanning bridge, which is carefully wheeled round and locked when any.oaoe leaveo the enclosure. The total space enclosed is about eight or nine acme, and this, excepting the pond, is thickly planted with trent, some of which are very old. The pond Itself covers an area of hardly more than an acre. It also is five-sided ; each of its anglffi ends in a ditch and this ditch itaelf terminated in the long fatal net. The question at onc,, arises, how do you get wild, ducks there? And this seems all the more difficult to ' answer from the circumstance that they are to rangy h. in England by ordinary travellers. But, as I ham said, England abounds with them, only they are adepts at keeping out iff night and taking care of themselv.. The owner of Eaton and with hint four other guns, on one 0W.4013 killed 2:52 wild ducks, including teal, is less than fur hours, and that nit far from Eaton Hall ; yet the district might have been travelled over fmm morning to night without hying a single one. But there 44 a more singular instance still of the way in ' which wild ducks avoid rapture. Often have I been paddled along a Canadian creek that ran through a marsh, and have known that there must be hundreds of ducks on the other side of the reeds and bulrusltio that shut out vast beds of wild rice, where the birds avere,no to My. sunning them- selvem in clover, for wild rice will bring ducks from any- where. ehouting or striking the canoe side with a paddle has not startled them In the least degree, but when the canoe hea passed along the ereek for half is furlong, and they were out of range, clouds of ducks have risen and flown away cackling; it used to sound to me like laugh- ing loudly. There i 4 a lake in a park rear Wittaborne, in Donetshire, which covers probably 120 acres, and this is never shot over under any circumstances It is admirably adapted for ducke, and they are SO tame that a visitor walking by it would in some seas°oo any that the owner was a wholesale poultry merehaut. I have even walked to the reeds at the water's edge, and the ducks only swam away. Yet outside the park where the lake is the ducks would be per- fectly wild. Now there is one special feature in wild duct., and that is their great curiosity. In the Canadian inarshes, where gnat bavi arcmade, but only by skil- ful and very qulck shots, it is in some parts customary to wave a bright red flag, and that will attract then ; but in the decoys a simpler attraetion is used. A small well-trained dog is employed to ruu over a given course. This 'he does till he has attracted the ducks into an enclosure, in which an ingenious net is laid down, and then the keeper shows himself at various points in succeseion till the ducks nec raptured. At Hale the principal dueks are mallards, teal, widgeon, and otyasionally pintails and scaup ducks. ! Mr. Mold, the head gamekeeper tn the Hale estate, told no that ducks I should certainty have expected to we, each as prehards or dun- birds or redheads, no they are iteliffereutly Me never taken, and golden eyes and gargeuy are nivally unknown. The decoy ducks are raised from the eggs of wild ducks, and they are fed on the pond regularly until they can fly away and entice their fellows into the pool, but never bv any chanty do they get into the long nets. Their motfve has often puetletl me, but I have now no doubt that it is thoughtlessnetin, for the keeper at Hale told UM that towards the end of the sea.eon the decoys will not go with the wild ducks to the entrance of the funnel or follow the attraction of the dog, but "Saws false," unit would doubtless appear front his view of the rasa These who have *hot ducks in Canada will have effinetimes noticed a single bird flying very rapidly at a great height in the air and disappearing in the dis- tance, unlike what we should expect from the gregari- ous habits of ducks, till it is Iffit to the range even of a telescope. The Atnerican pot Bryant, inn brautiful poem, speaks of it : Whither, 'midst falling dew, While glow the heavens with the last streaks of thy, Far thmugh their rosy depths, dost thou pursue Thy solitary way? Seeks% this the Itlashing brink of reedy the, Or maim at river wide. Or when. the rising billows heave and sink On the dtafed Ocean's Side ?

STANLEY, THE EXPLORER. (From "Men of the Time.-) Mr. Henry M. Stanley, was horn near Denbigh, in Wales, in 184 d. When three years old he was placed in the poor-house of Sr. Asaph, when. he remained ten years, and received an education which enabled him to teach in a school. At the age of fifteen he sailed as a cabindroy in a vessel bound for New Orleans. Here he was adopted by a merchant named Stanley, whose name lie took in place of his original one, which was John Rowlands. His patron died without leaving a will, and young Stanley was left to his own resources. Ile enlisted in the Con- federate army, and was made a prisoner, and subs, quently joined the Federal service, becoming a petty ' officer on a war-steamer. After the close of the war, he became a newspaper correspondent, and in 1867 was sent by the "New York herald" nails corres- pondent with the British Army in Abyssinia, and subsequently travelled in Spain and elsewhere. Ile WM finally sent by the conductor of the " herald" to find Dr. Livingstone, of whom nothing had been heard for more than two years. Stanley reached Zanzibar, on the east coast of Africa, early in J.., 1871, and on the :14th of October reached L pp, on Lake Tanganyika, where Livingstone had just arrived from the southwest. Stanley remained with , him until February, 1872, when Livingstone started , on tne journey from which he never returned, and , Stanley made his way back to Europe. The tele of this exploit induced the conductors of the "New ; York Herald " and of the London "Daily Telegraph " to send him, at their own expense, on another Arti- san expedition. Ile reached Zanzibar in the autumn of 1874, and learning that Livingstone was dead,ris- solved to go north-westward, and explore the re- gion of Lake Victoria :Vyanza. This, after many encounters with the natives, he reached in Feb. 1875, and found it to be the largest body of fresh , water on the globe, having an area of 40,1100 square miles. Ile then pushed west-ward towards Lake Albert N'yanza, and was able to satisfy himself that it was not, as had been generally supposed, con- nected with Lake Tanganyika. Forced by the hos- tility of the natives to return to t. pp, he deter- mined to decenel the great river discovered by Liv- ingstone, and believed by hitn to be the Nile, but which others thought was the Oingo ; and named by Livingstone the Luelaba, and by Stanley the , Livingstone. The descent, chiefly by canoes, occu- pied bun eight months, cost him the lives of thirty- live out of his one hundred and fifty men, and was accomplished under the greatest 'difficulties and privations. On reaching a settlement on the coast, a Portuguese national vessel took him to St. Paul de Loanda ; whence an English Vessel conveyed the party to the Cape of Good Hope, and thence to Zanzibar. Here his men were left at their home; and Stanley reached England in Feb. 1878. Ile has published an account of his first expedition, under the title" How I found Livingstone, 1872. Of his other expedition an acenillit is given in "Through the Dark Continent,' 1878. The President of the French Geographical Society presented the Cross of Chevalier of the Legion of Honour to Mr. Stanley at the Sorbonne, Paris, June 151. 1878. In 1879-82, lie visited Africa again, under the auspices of the -Uric. International Association founded at Brits-. eels. The object he bad in view was todevelop the great basin of the river Congo. The King of the Belgians devoted from his private purse .1:50,000 per annum towards this costl3, enterprise. and Stan- ley had practically unlimited means at his com- mand. Ile made a road on the side of the Living- stone Falls, with steamers on convenient level reaches, so as to reach Stanley P.I from Embom- ma. In Sept., 1882, a letter from Stanley was re- , ceived in London plated July 11), giving a brief account of his recent expedition to the Equator.; While Stanley was engaged under the Belgian Society political complications arose in consequence of the action of M. de Brum, who hoisted the French dog, and was said thus to imperil the free-! dom of the river Congo on the plateau above the • Cataracts. Tan members of the Warrington Braech if the English Cherub loam 110V0 e 000 out of their shell, though it cm hardly be feldel that they ham astonished the natives. They hell a meet- ing:it the Lien ll4tel, on Tuesday afternoon, and them was —for 411.41 a se,tion of the Churchh—a fairly good attmdance. The Rev. Cinon Hen ox occupied thethair, and spoke of " the formidable crisis in which the Caurffi of Eagland was placed." It will lie 1101,1 to lively of our mailers that the Church is in the throes of at crisis ; and lest s vno If thole should rush ti the conclu- -111011 that those wicked Dissenters have been at ! their old pranks—that is,agitating for disestablish- meld and disendownient —we hasten ti explain that the crisis has been brought about by the prosecution of the Dinner of Li >mots for Ritual- ism. Scene years ago, there was living in this country a heaven-sent statesman of the flaunt of IsAcoNsristo, whose cleath Churchmee mourn about this season of the year by making themselves gay with primroses. It was this same statesman who passed an at" to put down Ritualism ;" and it is this sanie act which is being brought into operation against the Bishop of Lincoln. It seems somehow as if things had got mixed. Cast it be that the great Beaconsfield was altogether wrong, 10111 if so what aliont the conjunction of the crisis in the Church and the primroses to his pious memory ? Perhaps 110010 prominent mem- ber of the English Church Union will explain— Mr. Joust Wiors,forinstance,for hem anauthonty, is he not ? on the English Church, Lord BEACONS. I PHILO, and the pale primrose. It is no 1150 con- tinning to pay tribute ti a nein who has brought a crisis on the Church, and for our part we will religiously refrain from sporting primroses en the Iffth April, if we can only be assured that to refrain is the right thing to do. But, meantime, what abont the proceedings against the Bishop ? Is it, after all, an epoch-making event that an odd Churclunan should he pms,cuted for conscience' sake? There are at this moment some scores of Irishmen lying in gaol for conscience sake. They have resisted had laws—especially made for the capture of Irishmen, and enforced by officials who take their cue from a vindictive Irish Secretary. Is there nothing to be said in their behalf ? Does this issue not amount to "a formidable crisis ?" The curious thing about the matter is that Tory Churchmen, when Irishmen are concerned, are for ever dinning it into our ears that the law must be obeyed, and that if these men choose to resist the low they inust take the consequences. Why do they not preach the 831111) Ilootrinn to the Bishop of Lincoln ? Is he, like tho wind, " a chartere d libertine ?" The Bishop has not yet, no far as we can hear, been compelled to herd with felons, or placed in a plank bed, Or had his hair clipped. Indeed, he has not been sent to gaol at all ; but is being proseented in a go-m-yoa-please style. He is the central tigare of what may be called an E,clesiastical Dobating Society, and is likely to emerge from the ordeal—such as it is —with-sit a hair turned or a vestment rufflml. We do not say it is wise to prosecute a dignatary of the Church, or that Ins lord- ship lansimm a fehm when he breaks the law: but we do nay that as an instance of suffering for conscience' sake his ease will bear no comparison with the p..rsecution at the present moment of the people of 'Maud. Boshles, the Bishop has the remedy in his own heads if he does not like the terms upon which he takes his thousands a year as an official, he can rid himself of his troubles by resigning his post. Not no with the Irishman; the • law is forced upon Win ; he may try to resign himself to it, but he cannot resign himself from it ; and in resisting the law it is not with him It miserable question of lighting candles and of man- millinery, but of standing by hearth and home and it wife and weans." Oh, that men would " elevate their vision," and perceive that the real crisis is not in the Church, but in the State, and that the remedy for it is to abolish coercion, and substitute I Home Rule.

div.head: BRUTALITY TO A. WIFE AT WIDNES.
div.p: BRUTALITY TO A. WIFE AT WIDNES.

At -Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. G. l'ilkington and 11. W. Deacon, an elderly man named John Newell was charged with unlaw- fully wounding his wife Bridget. Bridget Newell and she was the wife of the prisoner, and lived with his. at 31, Dickson-st. On Fridav morning, the sth inst., between five and six o'clock, sfie was with the prisoner in the kitchen. /le was getting ready to go to las work, while she was getting breakfast readv. The prisoner asked her who she was eutttrig bread -for, to which rho replied that she was rutting it for eJohnnie,'' the son, who was at that time in bal. The prisoner, who had at that time a slog in Isis stood up, and without any warning dealt her a violent blow on the head. Sho screamed out, and her son came downstairs, picked her up, and bathed her head. She gave her husband no provocation whatever. She was afterwards taken to the surgery of Dr. Ifutchirmin, where her wound was dressed. The prisoner was a man of violent character. :dm had twos married to him more than twenty years. She was afraid to live with him, as she could not trust hint. Iler head was now very had, and she felt weak. She had had mveral plumb with him, and on ono occassiou he broke her prisoner said his wife took a jug off the table and swore she wnuld split his skull with it. He never lot her with the clog at all. Ile gave her a push, and she fell against something and cut himself. (To his wilt:) Whatever you have got you deserve it ; it mimes you right.— Dr. Ilutehinisin said the woman came to hitn on Friday ;thaw half.past nine in the morning. She seemed we and faint faint loss of bloml. Her hair was matted with blmsl, and the side of her head was also covens]. Ho examined her, and found a contused wound on the upper and lack part of the head. It was over an inch in length, and penetrated to the bone. He dmssed her injury., and the wound MaR now improving. It would be about a week before Iter injury was better. A blow fmni one of the clogs produrnd would he likely to came the wound he saw. The wound being situate on the top of the head a fall could not be the case—F.C. Thompson said he apprehended the prisoner on Friday morning, I about half-past nine, in.Tictoria-road. Iletold him that , he wanted him for thong grievous bodily harm to his I wife, to whit% he replied, " don't believe her ; I never : touched her."—ln answer to the prisoner, witness said the son toll hitn that his mother was a bad one.—After Sewall had bran formally charged, he was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.

Mr. Chamberlain seems to have cleverly mis- managed things at Birmingham. " Oh," as Sir Lucius 07ligger would say, 'its a very pretty quarrel as it stands." Mr. John Croalield saw what was coming a couple of years ago, when ,writ- ing to Mr. Gladstone, he soul—" Mr. Chamberlain has tried to trip you up, mid lie will bud himself on his back.-

There woo a time when the member for West Birmingham wan the pride of the Radicals. He bolted at a critical moment, and has since basked in the smiles of Prininsie dames, and feasted his soul with applause at Tory-Unionist meetings. Ho is lost to the Liberals ; and the Tories of Birmingham make —oh, such remarks ! when his name is mentioned, There are " none no poor as to do hini reverence."

div.head: WARRINGTON V. LEIGH.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. LEIGH.

The Warringtonians having an cpen date on Saturday arrangements were mado to play Leigh. A special train was run from Warrington, conveying more 900 persons to the scene of action, whilst others took advantage of the fine afternoon, and trade the journey by road. Both teams were exceptionally strong, anti at 3.45 Smith started operations. Barnes met the kick off with a misty to half way, and from the succeeding line out Nevins and Povey dribbled will info the Leigh quarters. Even play followed bere until Jolley made a desperate effort to break through the home defence,Sinith just tack- ling him in time. Massey and Worthington exchanged kicks, but still the Leigh men could not clear. However, aidssl by short rushes and the judicious kicking of thelf backs, the home:item managed to gain a foothold in the Warrington twenty-live, lost Dillon and Littlowsiod removed hostilities-by Into ling the oval to half way. Coop frustrated a movement of the Warrington forwards by a 1 ttt ge punt into touch, and Leigh stsicSl MOM attacked. A penalty kirk sermsl as relief to the visiting side, but the Leigh moor miss Hot te, he denied, and fear. a line out Gorman srsturvi, and having a clear opening daShVI ovet the line and gainvl the first tangible point of the game. Coop took the place, but failed to convert. This reverse seemed to rouse the Warringtonians tn renewed efforts, for on Fair Turner's drop-out a hasty visit was at once paid to the Leigh sin:seers. A wild pass from Smith to Corm almost ended in disaster to the Leigh side, but the es-iFottington player cleared his goal in marvellous fashion, and the dangs‘r was averted. Barnes put in some grand work, and called forth lostd cheers for a really brilliant run and kick. Jolly now essayed a drop at goal, but the MB was ton low, and Coop touched down. No relief was brought through the dnspsint, for Randles got clear away Man a lino out and passed all opposition, but Coop raced after ilk man, bringing him down a yard from the line. Still Warring- ton attacked, and relief was brought by Worthington conceding a minor. Another minor followed thmogh Speakman's kick. The play now resolved itself to neutral ground for a vonsiderable period, lint Massey made his mark, to which Hurst only feebly risponded. Fair Turner and Litt lewood prevented (Vas risisincling to a kick of Evans, and Dorn a writ:linage Speakman, Antrubus, and Alassev passed neatly, the three-quarter compelling a minor IT a long kirk. Foul tackling of Barnes awarded the visitors a free kids, and again the Leigh goal woo innocent. The Warrington c•mtre now tried a drop at grril, but with the .1110 rrsult as his pre- demriors, and the lifth minor was nigistered. The visitors still plodded on fearlsssly with the hope of gain- ing the lead. Eventually th••ir efforts were rewarded, for Spettkman stir-a- across the pack to Antroblis, who cleverly evaded the opposing hair husks. Being pressed Ire threw to Dillon, who slritslied well and emssing to Massey the last-named pickel iip in grand fashion. and finally suececiled in kiwering the Leigh goal. This sue- ems of the Warringtonions was received with loud cheers by their supporters. Leigh restarted from centre and at once made tracks for the Warrington goal. The unitsri efforts of Names, Jolley, Speakman, and Antrolins frustrated them, and half time was reached with the score as follows—Warrington One goal and five minors,to Leigh one try. Fair Turner resumed hostilities, and the game at once became of that exeiting nature which had charac- terised the first portion. Antrobim got away Dons the pack. and threw the oval between Barnes and Massey. Worthington intercepted and raced down the fichl, and, cleverly evading Evans mid Massey, wound up as ant run by scoring. Coop failing at the place, Dillon and Ashton rushed the oval down the field soon after Turner's dropssut, but still the home defenco Was not to be tampered with. J. l'endlebury put ins spirited run, only to finds hurler in Jolley. The last nanusl now put in a grand run along the popular side, and his efforts were ably seconded by the neat passing of Spmkinan, Antrirbse•, Barnes, and Alaswy, the latter finally punting into touch at the Loin)] quarter flag. Hurst cleared Iris lines at a stritical moment, but Massey more than equalised a run of Worthington's by a huge , punt to the half way flag. Evans was called moin to defend his charge, which he assemilitlished in creditable Ifashion, but a rush by the Leigh f•srwardsrestulted in a 'minor. Worthington compelled as second minor point Iby a smart kick. A grand ;rush los Dillon, Ashton, ' Unsworils, and Turner took the oval to the half way • flag, and the ball I:miming loose a race ensued between Manor and Worthington. The first-named reached the oval first, and got in a flying kick, but unfortunately Worthington failed to stay his career, and charging MasssT the Warringtonian was no seriously injured that . he was carried off ths- field. This sad :misfortune cast a , damper on the whole, processli tt gs, and words of con- dolence were expressed for Massey, who had up tsi the lilac isf his accident Ls-en playing a remarkably fine game, and had establishes] himself a famturite wills tile , large assemblage. linsworth was taken front the pack , to till the vacancy in this back division. Worthington ran and dodged in grand style, Fair Turner checking his career. Barnes got the leaths•r away in marvellous • fashion,but exchange kicks resulted in another ininor to • the homestrirs. Gorman sconsl again for the hoineteam, Smith failing at an easy pltsee. Barnes put in same , grand defensive work towards theelose, and time afts•r time frustrattsl the efforts of Hist Leigh men to score. ' Thu game was now practically osn•r, and Mr. Bleackley's whistle brought a WeieolllP rclii•f, the final result • reading soar draw, Warrington having scored rise , 'five minors, to Leigh three tries and five minors,

Thi play during the first half wasof a first class churn- tee, but during the second half there WAS a considerabla I falling off in the dash of the Warringtonians that has characterind their play during the whole of the past season. This fact can easly be accounted for—several of the players were more or lex; injured, and after Massey's ar,ident, the Warringtonians played a cautious game rather than rttn heading into disaster. Evan.s played fairly well at full back, but all the three-quarters displayed rare form all through the march. Barnes put in some grand defensive work towanls the close, whilst both Jolley and Ilaswy ran and biked with excellent judgment. Antrobus and Speakman never nagged in the least, whilst in the forward division it would be a hanl task to snake a disfinetion.

During- the -last few months the Rev. Edward Sandys Jackson, M.A.. has been in foreign parts recruiting hi, health, and has very much benetttted thereby. It is now some ten years ago since the reverend gentleman became Vicar of Great Sankey, and took up his abode in that parish, and during that time he has succeeded in greatly endearing hitnself to his Hock, and to many others in the parish who are not counted amongst the number of those who attend his church. ender his charge many useful works received an impetus, and he inns had a great deal to do with the restoration of , the church of St. Mary's, the building of new! schools, and the building of a mission room at Penketh. It is not, therefore, to he wonderel at that when his health began to show gigne of giving! way his 'wrist:loners took alarm, and eagerly ; assented to his project of departing for a warmer clime, in the hope that lie might return not only safe and sound, but much improved so far as the ! innate of his health was coneemed. Though they regretted his absence, they were reconciled to it, and when at last Mr. Jackson returned it was very promptly decided that his welcome home should be no ordinary one. The outcome of this b.:solution was the drawing ail of an aoldnwo of congratulation to the reverend gentleman one his return in renewed health and vigour, which carried the signatures of nearly 350 parishioners,and the ladiesdnover behindoliand in tnatters of this sort, clubbed together on their own account to present to their Vicar sonsi substantial tokens of their rega rd. The "tokens" took the shape of a walking, itch, a reading desk, and an easy chair, and Otto address is handsomely bound in Persian leather, and is illutni- nabs!. On the cover, in solid gold, is the monogram of Mr. Jackson, and on the timt page is a repre.ntation : nit his coat-of-a row, associated with those of his college yublln.

THE RICH TRAMP AT WARRINGTON. A "BUSINESS " PROPOSAL. With regard to the tramp who recently sought admittance to the Warrington Workhouse with over .£lOO in his possession. the Workhouse Master (Mr. Ward) reported to the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday that the man bad been . taken to the Workhouse hospital. The report of the master was in thefol lowing terms "Admitted from t eviagrsntwueclJo, Load,aged 56. as he could not get any further, as he was suffering from Ind legs and swelling of the body. Ile had in las piesession when admitted to the tramp ward £lOO in notes, £7 in gold. 13a 6d. in silver, Is. 30. in copper— total. £lO7 a 4. 90. A few days ago the Workhouse Master received a letter in which was enclosed the printed business card of "Holmes and Sons. ironmongers and furniture dealers," of Sydenhant, together with the following note, signed "P. Holmes " addressed to himself " Having seen the account in the newspaper; of the tramp artio had entered your workhouse with £lO7 will : you kindly give him the enclosed letter and oblige." Thel enclosed letter read as follows :- 1 122, Wens-mid, dydenham, April 6, 1889.—Sir,—I am 1 in want of a partner with small eapital—£3o would be I sufficient. I have been established many Years and always buy for cash at sales, but business is now 1 ineirasing and money and help are both wanted. You 1 earl take an active part in the business and live here rent free and ham a comfortable house. the house being equal to my own property ; having no rent to pay there I is no liability whatever and a certain fortune for you. I shall be premed to hear from you. I am living quite near the Crystal Palace, and this place is healthy and you will soon get strong and well. I have my wife and family living with me.—Youtu truly, P. Holmes. It is,perhaps, hardly necessary to say that we have not as yet heard of any partnership arrangements being entered into.

The Halifax Morning Herald (Nova Scotia, Canada), of October Bth, 1888, contains the following interesting letter :--

div.head: Pathetic Narrative by a Steamship Fireman.---His Sufferings in a Foreign Hospital.---Manly Gratitude to His Mysterious Benefactor.
div.p: Pathetic Narrative by a Steamship Fireman.---His Sufferings in a Foreign Hospital.---Manly Gratitude to His Mysterious Benefactor.

MR. Eorroa,---It may seem like presumption in me to write a letter for publica- tion, as lam but a poor workman without education. But while I was ill in the Victoria Hospital at Halifax, and given up to die by the doctors, a lady came to me and gave me a medicine that cured me. I don't know her name or where she lives.
An angel from Heaven couldn't have done more for me. I want this letter printed in hopes that she may, by chance, see it and know lam well and remember her. When
she reads the following history of my ease she will recognise me as the poor dying man she saw in that hospital and know that I have not forgotten her great goodness to me.
RICHARD WADE.
GLASGOW, Sep. 10, 1888.
been a fireman. Quite often I would be sick and feel like vomiting and had more or less
pain in the right side and in the head. The skin of my face and bands got a yellow colour, too, as I have seen plenty of people have in India and elsewhere in tropical countries.

"A man who has been strong and hearty all his life is slow to believe he is really ill, and so it was with me. It was two months before I gave up work, on getting home from a voyage. Hardly had I set foot on shore before I felt in a manner ashamed of giving up, and convinced myself that it was only a cold, and I should be all right in a few days. Cheered up by this idea, though I was not a bit better, two or three days after I landed I sailed again in the steamship, Concordia,' of the Donaldson line, for Baltimore. Early on the passage I was taken worse. My stomach swelled, and I had several bad attacks of vomiting, besides all the symptoms that had troubled me before. We reached Halifax in thirteen days, and I was left in the Victoria General Hospital
there, and the ship sailed away without me. The House Surgeon, Dr. Jacques, gate
me some powders to stop the vomiting. Next (lay the Visiting Physician came in and examined me; he gave me a mixture to take every four hours. I took it a few times, hut
as I felt a great deal worse I stopped biking the powders. When Dr. Lathim called to see me the next day he saw that I was so ill he told the nurse to stop giving me the
mixture also. lie gave me no more medicine during his month, and I assure you that
I was not sorry when the time came for him to take his departure. In the meantime I lay fearfully ill, and getting worse every day, and had small hopes of ever seeing
home again.
"After this physician went away, Dr. Campbell came; he was Visiting Physi-
cian to the Hospital for the next five months. He gave me other medicines, but not much relief. Nearly all that time I was in great torture.
No food that I took would
digest in my stomach; I vomited up everything I ate. There was a terrible pain in my bowels, a burning heat in my throat, heartburn and headache. I was taking a

mixture every four hours, powders one after each meal to digest the food, operating pills one every night, temperature pills two each night, to stop the cold sweats, and after all these fine medicines the appetite was getting worse every day, and I was a
poor miserable man. Then I got cold, and took the pleurisy in the left side, and after
ten weeks of suffering I took it in the right side; and then the doctors performed an
operation, and took ninety ounces of matter from my right side. Then they told me I
would never get over ii; I must die.

"After Dr. Campbell's five months were up, we got another Visiting Physician; he gave me a mixture to take three times a day, and this, I assure you, had a terrible effect on me. It made me tremble like a leaf on a tree. Then I stopped all their medi-
eines at once. I said if I must die, I could die just as well without them. By this

time I was so far gone that I could not take a drink of milk without it would turn sour and lie on my stomach for days. My flesh had wasted away, and I was like the wreck of a ship fast on a shoal waiting for the sea to beat it to pieces.

"When I was in this state, one day a lady I had never seen came to the hospital She proved to be an Angel of Mercy, for without her I should not now be alive. She told me of two medicines, called Mother Seigel's Cura- tive Syrup and Mother Seigel's Operating Pills, and brought them to me next day. I started with the Syrup, taking twenty drops after eating, and took the Pills by the directions on the box. Ix only a few days' time I was out of bed calling for ham and egcs for breakfast. From that time I kept on with Mother Seigel's medicines, and got well fast, and soon was able to leave the hospital and came home to Glasgow. I feel no pains of any kind; I feel as if I was in another world, and soon expect
and saw and talked to me.

to go to work once more. I have had to take no operating medicine since I began to get the effect of the Syrup. How surprised and thankful lam I have not the words to tell, but I wish you would publish this statement, poor as it is, that all the people may know what to do for troubles like mine.

div.head: HIS PERSONAL STATEMENT.
div.p: HIS PERSONAL STATEMENT.
"I am not used to writing and may not be able to make the reader take the
same interest in my story as Ido myself. But I feel it my duty to lay it before the
public, and all I need to say in advance is that what I am going to place on record is
the pure and simple truth—l have nothing to gain by altering a single fact.

"My name is Richard Wade, and I live at No. 244, Stobeross Street, Anderston, Glasgow, where I pen these words. For the past fourteen years I have been sailing out of the port of Glasgow as fireman on different lines of steamships. For six years I was in the Anchor Line Mail Steamers between Glasgow and New York, but for the most of the time I have been on steamers in the Bombay and Calcutta, China and South American trades. Although the work of a fireman on these great ships is very hard

and exhausting and uses up most of the men that follow it in a short time, I had always been strong and healthy until about a year ago. Then for the first time I began to feel weak and ill. My appetite failed and I suffered from heartburn; I felt dull and sleepy and not like work; there was a bad taste in my mouth and I noticed my tongue was coated. My stomach felt dead and heavy and my bowels were no longer regular as they had been before. Sometimes when at work I would have a slight fit of dizziness come over me, that I thought might be the effect of the heat in the fire-room, yet I asked myself how could that be when I had never felt it before in all the many years I had

div.head: tetterl to the Obitor.
div.p: tetterl to the Obitor.
•• GRANDMOTHERLY LEGISLATION?'

Sir,—Who to" Vindex" of Earlestown ? He seems to be. Daniel come to judgment, abd trim to be satin- cal. If it be right to keep liquor shops opun for the benefit of suck dry souls as he, why should his wife and family be excluded from the benefits? Surely it is supremely selfish on his part to object to his wife and " fine family of girls and boys " copying his example— and thus enjoying a "booze "as well as himself. Presi- dent Lincoln said :—`• Slavery is either right or wrong. If it be right, we ought to defend and uphold tI if it he wrong, we ought to destroy it- The liquor traffic is either good or had. II it be good, then it ought to be marled on openly and freely like other useful trades ; if it is had. and at war with virtue, morality, education and religion, then it ought to be prohibited in the in- terests of law, order, and good government, even though " Vindes " should call it "Grandmotherly." If he objects to laws that are violated, what law will es- cape repent? Because the prohibition of the liquor trade on Sunday leads certain vicious persons to form clubs for tic purpose of drinking illegally, are we to pander to these people? Every thoughtful man will answer—" No." The law mtmt be enforced and wrong- doers punished. An act of Parliament will not make people such as " %Index " goal ; but it will serve to prevent them from doing much harm. The licensing laws are the most vicious and immoral on the statute book, and they must be overthrown. The facts in favour id the Suntkiy elating of liquor shops are no, strong and numerous that they cannot be controverted. The Womach of Yindex "is stronger than his brains. fle M evidently, from his style and gouge, not much in favour with good things, and his re- ference to " tiod's gifts " displaym his ignorance, while his slaps at Sir W. Lawson and Sir William Harcourt only reveal his fossil Toryism. The " Fanatics and Fad- no, styled, have .succiieded, and will continue to succeed in their efforts to render the social and other life of England more punt and enjoyable, and if " %Index " can't endure it, he must "grin and bear it R. 9 he does the dry sermon, or, if it will suit him better, let him , emigrate. Our home life will lose nothing that is sober, pure, and good from his alto-nee. Any person who at this time of the day believes that prohibition of the puts lie and common sale of intoxicating drinks on Sunday, will" increase family drinking and the debauchinent of home," and the " neglect of the Sanctuary," is beyond the reach of reason and COMITIOII sense, and ought to introduced to the govenor of (Within, i.e. if his "grand- mother " ig not alive to muse and care for lihn. It is to be hoped that when he next ventures to appear in print he will have the courage to sign his name, to that we may know hiin.—Yours

ANOTHER GOAL JO 111'NCORN.

Sir,—l notice on reading the doings of our worthy Commissioners at their lust meeting, reported at length in your valuable issue of last week, the members have unanimon,ly a„oreed, after a few of the must loquacious had delivered themselves of sundry tempestuous speeches, to increase the stipend of their Secretary from £175 to £2OO a year. I am sure the must premed rate- payer—if there is such a being to to. found in Runcorn now-a-days—will not begrudge this, for, according to the unanimous testimony of the Board Mr. Nl:lnitial' is the " right man in the right " Rooks always ready for auditor. No surehargea as in days gone by." I" Hear, hear)" from all the members. Now what strikes roe very forcibly is this—if the ratepayers consider the assistant overseer's stipend rJetuld be raised to £250 year, why 8110U111 not the salary of the secretary to the Board,whose dutiesare, I should think, much more ono, ous,be raised to at !fast diesame amount? I notice thatone of the members in discussing the !natter got mill, 'lliSt'll and sot tiled to drift into a fog, talking rather incoherently t.l the proverbial abilities of a Philadelphia lawyer. fle, however, mentioned that some of their officers lately got urine of 82 per cent. I fancy this must orely apply. to the Roard's officers who brush 'the stiwts, und who, I am inforined,have to try and eke out • miser-

able existence on the paltry pittance of half-a-crown a slay. I believe the Board's worthy sorveyor, who, with- out doubt, is the Noah of their Ark, did 'get an advance very recently of £95 a year; but every rateisayer bows Intl wcll how richly In deserved it. : Now, I think if the Board would pay a uniform rate of wages, say the Surveyor £lO and all their other officers down to, and including, •' Jim " Percival, the Nuisanee Inspector, the sum of £5 a week each, the Board.:would require to lose no more of their precious time cobbling ! and patching at salaries for some little Om, to come. I Let their wages be paid weekly,aay at noon evety Friday, ! no that the officers might be able to send their set-rants . to Market early, before the choicest cuts disappeared. ! • .. "

I ant sorry t notice that the much talked 4 improve- ments which wen' about to be made in such gisual style at the eelebrated Waterloo Bridge have again vanished into thin air. This is just what I expect's' would take place ; another £lOO of the ratepayers' money needlessly thrown away. Mad the f'ononissioners placed the matter entirely and onreservedly in OW hands of their own able surveyor, instead of going elsewhere, and generously allowed him to cope his almady IMMO.un laurels with this little piece of architecture, I hel sure ere this this job would have been beautifully and satisfactorily cone pleted. Surely we have talent enough at home competent to draw the plan of a small arch bridge and show its 'punt itieS,tll cross an old canal not much bigger than an iirdinarycnuntry ditch. Talkalxiut leaving •• foidprints in the sands of time, " why we have miles on miles of beautiful streets am' avenues, in and about our gnind old town, with footprints innumerable—in winter at any rate.—Yours, Runcorn, April 1.00, 1889.

div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL LATCHFORD. . _ . .

The Latchford section enntinuen to be a scene of great activity, the work here being more in connection with the railway rmbanklnent than with the canal itself. The embankment is being raised and lengthened very rapidly, several locomotives and numerous wagons being engaged in the work. All this is not donne without trmsiderable inconvenience to the residents in the neighbourhood, and to those who frequent the roads intersected by the contractor's lines of metals. This inconvenience has been no severely felt that we understand that a meeting of residents in Latchford will shortly he held to con- sider the desirability of approaelting the Ship Canal Company, or Mr. Walker, the contractor, with reference to the danger of the temporary railwayn, the smoke and noise from the engines, the annoyance Calbled by /night working, the alteration of roads and other matters c. nested with the making, of the Ship Canal as far as Latchford in affected thereby. The circular convening the meeting, has been signed by Councillor Edward (treenail, jun., Councillor F. A. Iloberts, Major Litton, 3.1'., and Councillor John White, JP.

A LEGAL ISSUE. In the Chancery Division yesterday week, before Mr. lJustice Chitty, Mr. Romer, Q.C. appeared with the Attorney-General in support of a motion in the action the Atternev-lieneral v. The Manchester Ship Canal Company, and said that it had been arranged between the parties that it Should stand over. The motion is for an injunction to restrain the Maneliester Ship Canal Company from making embankments of the river Mersey above the line shown in the plan and sections, which were signed by Sir W. Forster, and referred to in tho Manchester Ship Canal Act, of 1885. The motion also sought to restrain the Canal Company from making openings in the emlxmlunents otherwise than in aecordance with the plans and section. The counsel engaged in thrones. are the Attorney-General (Sir R. Webster, Q.C., M.P.) Mr. Romer, QC., Mr. U.S. Wright, Mr. Ingle Jerre, Sir Horace Davy, Q.C., M.P., Mr. Henn Collins, &LC., and Mr. L E. Clare.

In the Queen's Ilench, London, no Monday, thorns.. of Dibson v. Mackie came before Justima Denman and Stephm, sitting as a Divisional Court.—Mr. C. A. Russell explained that he appeared in summrt of the appeal of Mr. David Mackie, of Crewe, and Mr. Henry Roddinetrin, of Strangeways, against two orders of Mr. Justice Matthew, making absolute an order charging a liniment obtained Isy a plaintiff in December last against the defendant Mackie upon certain Mares in the Manchester Ship Canal which were mid to belong to the defendant. The learned counsel stated that on thelilth of January last Mr. Oshorn obtained on an ex poen application an order ahi charging tile 01,01,4 in the Ship Canal Coinimny with his ifebt. The 21st of the same month was the date fixed for showing imuse against the order, but on the 16th the plaintiff's mlicitor agreed to the matter being adjourned until February 4th. Not. withstanding thitt consent, on January 21st the plaintiff attended before Mr. Justice Mathew ; the Manchaftvr ship Canal Company was mprivented. but no one appeared for Mr. Mackie. Justice Mathew mails. an , otter atsolute against the ilefendant Mackie and the Ship Canal Company charging the shares and extending the t i•ne for showing cause n sip port of s,sidington to February 4th. A RATEPAYER.

THE INVACCINATION OF LEPROSY. Sir,—Kepeated complaints have been made in the West Indies that the public health is being gradually undertnined by the. propagation of the most loathsome and intractable ef all diseases, and in spin. of warnings and remonstrances on the part of resident medical practitioners and others, no serious attempt has been tuadetee cope with the evil. Cl,, the contrary, the results of a medical inquiry made by a circular Issued about two years ago, by direction of His Excellency Governor Robinson, rlf Trinidad, in which evidence of the evil is demonstrated, have not even been. disclosed, still less acted upon. That leprosy is seriously menquiag through- out the West Indies and in British Gniana is not disputed hy anyone who has taken the tneuble to examine the facts or institute ate inriniry. The Leper Hospitals an. everywhere full to overfinwing, and lepers have to be received at nearly, if not all, the general or colonial hospitals t ana these hapless victims an. met with in even grade of society. In some islands there are leper villages or communities which are cons stantly increasing. On expressing astonishment during my recent visit, at a statement made toter by an old resident physician at Demerara as to the widespread character ett this repulsive affliction, my informant (referring ton reception and ball to he held that I,voning in honour of the(iovernor of the Leeward Islands) added, , I know some hpers who will he present and mix with , the gay throng this evening." It is admitted that lien, dity and insanitation can only be held responsible for . part of this inerease..and the theory of contagion k resorted to as affordeng a pessible explanation of the difficulty. I have, however. visited several hospitals and larareths where medical practitioners, nurses, laundresses, and attendants have Isrm regularly employed for periods varying from five to twenty. years (in one instance 33 years), coming inn. the closest contact with the unfortunate inmates, and on Asking special inquiries on the point, I could net learn IA a single case of infection no communicated. Two coins mittees of the Royal College of Physicians, after full investigation, deny the contagimes character tef the dis- ease in foto. On the other hand, most authorities., including several medical superintendents of leper asylums, admit th..t. like other ennstitutional diseases, leprosy is inoculable, and it is alleged the only way in which inexmlation is systematically practiced, and ono scale large enough to account for the growing evil, is by vaccinatinn. Intelligent observers in all ranks of society have declared with the uttnost frankness at their belief that this increase, in part at all events, is due to vaceination, and some of then) testify to the disgusting maJatly (one a member of the legislative Council) having been inoculated into the blood of their own healthy children, ruining them for life. As a coos, eptence, despite laws in some Colonies, they steadfastly refuse to incur the like perils for their other children, and resort to various seratagems for their prott.ction. In the Islands of Grenada and St. Kitts leprosy was almost unknown previous to the intneduction of comptilsory . vaccination. It is now a common malady. In tieorge. town, British Guiana, the dread of leprosy is to general that the vaccination law has become to a large degree a dead letter. Vaccination. moreover, it need hardly he observed, is a much more harardons operation in the torrid sone, owing to the effects of climate on the vaccine virus, and the particu- lars of thnee fatal cones occuring in Trineviad were reported to me in one day. In every part of die West Indies it is no exaggeration to say that the woos lireall vaccination, but being practically (except in Barbados) withoot represnitation, they have no means of redress. Many have urged use to make known this intolerable grievance through the English press, and I venture to hope that you will nspond to their reasonable appeal by the insertion of this communication. Yours faithfully. Devonshire Club, St. James's, London.
TEHH.

When the nutter ionic Oil again on the 4th February Justice Matthew made tho iodor absolute, but said he could not deride whether the shares helongml It Boddington or not. To find that out he said there [oust bean issue tried, with Roddiugton as plaintiff and Gibson as defendant. He (Mr. Russell) contended that the charging order ought to be dischargid pending the trial of the ison. Mr. ned- dington Imught the shares tof Mackie in dilly, 1884. The first transfer wan invalid ; the second transfer could not be carried through owing to the illness of one of the parties. That was how the shares continued to be in the name of Mackie. Gaskell jun.. a , boy named William Thomas, was charges with working a mule whilst in an unfit state ; and W. , King, farmer, Ilalebank Farm, was charged with causing the mule to be worked P.C. Ilalebronk deposed that on the dud inst., about half-past six in the evening, lie saw is mule attached to a milk cart in Victoriemad. Tile boy was driving. Ile stoppsl the cart opposite Mr. Martley's shop, and exammel the mule. On the leftshoulder he found a raw wound the Sin of a five shilling pitee, and therewas another wound on the animal's back about the size of the bible (Pro- &iced). In one of its load legs was a hots into which , Ito could easily insert two fingers. The animal woo in very poor vondition and lie had never seen a warse case ! of cruelty sin, he had been in the force.—lnspector Nicholls, It.S.P.C.A., said ho examined the mule at the farm on the 4th inst, lie corn.borated the Constable's statement as to the wounds, and said the animal was in poor condition and quite unfit to work. The boy told him he worked the mule because he was sent with it. The boy added that he bathed the wounds on Tuesday morning, and his master bathed the wounds on Monday morning. Witless informed the defendant King of this statement, which he denied.—The defendant said he was away on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, and lie was not aware the mule had son, The bov hail no right tn, work it as there were two horses in the stahle which were perfeetly right —The Bench dismissed the summons against the hoe. on payment of costs &s. ........ .... In connection with the Runcorn WesleyanCircutt Temperance Society, Mr. Thomas Hardy, ot Liver- pool. I lecturer from the United Kingdoms Alliance, has conducted a vigorous campaign in Runcorn; and it is believed that his efforts will bear good fruit in the future. Sir. Hardy commenced pro- ceedings in St. Paul's Chapel, on Sunday afternoon, when he preached a powerful sermon dealing with the religious aspect of the temperance question. There was a good congregation. On Monday even- ing he was one of the principal speakers at a meet- ing in Camden Chapel, and at the same place on Tu.- day evening hedelivered a lecture, entitled "Tile nature add object of our work." The Rev. It. Burson Mellod the duty of chairman. On Wednesday evening a nume- rous audience assembled in Brunswick Sunday. School, Mr. Hardy on this Ileei.loll dealing with the subject id •• Drunkiird4' sacrifices.- Mr. John Simpson occupied the chair, and in the course of an earnest address, tont so far as his experience went, having tried takings little drink for upwards of 50 years and then for [Jae last 12 or 13 years never having taken anything at all, he odd say, whenever a medical man arivised the taking of drink as a beverage, "lost believe Mtn." (Applause.)—He Was certain it would not do them the slight.t god, and however little they took it would do them mnore or loss harm, and if they once commenced to take drink as a bevi.rage, where they woold stop no man I could tell. mApplassi.)—He believed the only safe plan ' was not to take any drink at all and wi h regard to his ; experience he omid say he was better Icohily, mentally, ! and spiritually and in every way. (Applause.)—There was another large audience on Thursday evening I when the Rev. J. Judson took the chair and Mr. Hardy lectured on mt Drunkenness, a disease ; its caws., and cure.- Last evening another capital meeting was held and a resolution in favour of local option was carried with enthusiasm. An efficient choir had been present at each meeting and appropriate hymns have been sung, and Chooe present have heartily joined in the vocal exercisex. An important part of Mr. Hardy's work has been the holding of mid-day meetings at :the various works in the town. Working-men have gathered in large numbers and Mr. Hardy, who is a ready and witty speaker, has delivered SUMS convincing speeches in favour of total abstinence.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY "OCC.HONALCORRESPONDENT."

'That those who follow the reports of Parliament- ary proceedings will notice that our member, Mr. Brunner, is very regular and con•tant in his attend- ance at the House of Commons, and never fails to record his vote on any important division. A marked instance of his close attention to the , nation's business took place during the week end- ing March 29th. lie was in the House of Commons each glay and racer led his vote in 13 divisions out of 14 which took place. This far eclipses the record of any other Cheshire member. He voted with Mr. Cremer in his motion opposing the additional expenditure on the navy. That the Runcorn Board of Commissioners have debated the question whether a law clerk is neces- sary for the proper transaction of the town's business, and they have decided in the affirmative. The appointment lies between Mr. A. Linaker, brother of the late law clerk, and Mr. P. A. bake, and it is said that the latter gentleman, who has been a most useful member of the Board for the past six years, will he the chosen one, by a substantial , majority. , That the Waterloo Bridge Committee are evidently ' believers in the aphorism "Assume a virtue if you have it not.' The cool and easy manner in which they passed over their miserable failure to deal with the subject, metaphorically patted each other on the back tor their assiduous care and their res- traint in not spending £4,000 of the ratepayers' money, was surprising. The subject has been on the (epic for about ten years, and it is as far from settlement as ever, and if the committee meets only once in eight months, as has once been the case, will not be settled this century. That the 2100 paid to Messrs. Holmes ions much good money thrown in the gutter. That the discussion on Sunday trains was highly diverting if not exactly edifying, and the incident related by Mr. Pritchard was mirth-provoking in the highest degree. A gentleman of a respectab/e position in the town was on his way to Widnes on !Sunday to catch a train and,being informed that an attempt was to be made to obtain such a con- venience in Runcorn, Inc holds up his hand in holy horror and descants upon the demoralising tendency of Sunday trains. Mr. Pritchard must bring better arguments than these if the people are to be con- vinced of the iniquity of travelling on Sunday. That Sunday is the only day the working classes have altogether at liberty and it is the favourite day for visiting relatives and friends that live at a distance, and also for spending a few houra that , are brighter and fairer than Runcorn and Widnes. I And where is the harm of taking the journey on the I seventh day of the week, ordinary mortals fail to per- ceive. Mr. Imison was alarmed lest the a orking- men would be tempted to spend more than they could afford but they may be safely left to decide i that question for themselves and will be found not to overstep the mark. That the number of people who cross Runcorn I Bridge on Sundays in order to get a train at Wid- , Iles it, very considerable and as there are railway lines laid in Runcorn and trains now pass through : the station morning and evening, it is a lianlship that the townspeople Amid be put to the incon- venience and discomfort of a walk of two miles. .

That kit hoped the Committee appointed will succeed in getting the Bridge fare reduced, about the excessiveness of which all are agreed, and also in arranging trains at convenient times on Sunday. That in the Widnes Local Board election and in the Guardians election Mr. Brouchemite's defeat was complete and disastrous and ought to deter him from again entering the lists. That Dr. O'Keeffe is to be congratulated upon the success he achieved in heading the poll.

In aid of the fund established with the object of obtaining an organ for the Runcorn United Methodist Free Church, the sacred cantata, "Esther, the beautiful queen," was performed in Unicorn Public Hall on Monday evening, and a large and appreciative audience assembled to hear the 11111AiC and help the good cause. Mr. John Holton!, who hal undertaken the direction of the . concert, had gathered together a powerful choir of laJ voices,the effect being considerably heightened I by the presence of an admirable orchestral band under the leadership of Herr Praeger, of Warrington. The persons represented in the cantata were : Esther, the Ibleen, Mrs. Newell ; Ahasuerus, the King, Mr. Arthur Pox; Haman, Mr. L. (lidded by the baton of Mr. Holfonl, the choir rendered a good account of , themselves, especially in the concluding chorus 1" Praise ye the Lord," which bad to be repeated. The cantata was also performed in Free Church schoolroom, Oak/and-st., Widnes, on Wednesday ' evening. with the object of reducing the debt on that building. There was a good audience. The principals were unchanged, but the ehorus had been considerably reduced,in order to suit the dimensions ,of the building. Mr. 11. S. Timmis performed the functions of chairman.

The Special Comniission Corset was crowded yesterday morning, when Sir Charles Russell resumed his address. lle askiel the Court to contrast the eviden, in its weak. nes. and generality with the sprite, weighty, and grovirms charges that the Land League leaders Irtd based their movement on assassination and outrage. The hostility of the governing minority was the highest tribute to Mr. Parnell's worth. This inquiry had been Mr. Pamell's vindication. Ile and his friends were now the accusers and not the accused. Concluding an impassioned peroration, Sir Challis hoped this inquiry would remove misconceptions and ha.sten reconciliation; that there would be dispelled for ever the cloud which had rested on the noble reign and undimmed glory of a mighty empire Their lordships then adjourned until the 30th of April. H•RCOURT said there could be no doubt now but that the policy of the Government was extermination aided by the battering ram, which was constructed for knock- ing shown the houses of the wretchedly pwr who could not pay rent.— The Chancellor of the Exchequer denied thatthe policy of the Government was extermination. Battering rams, he contended, were more humane than boiling water.—Mr. %win condemned the use of batter- ing mns.—After ohnervations from Mr. Sexton, Colonel Nolan, Mr. J. Stuart, Mr. T. I'. O'Connor, Mr. G. M. W. Wane, the motion for adjournment of the House on Tues- day next for Easter holidays NEM agreed to.

MR. BRIGHT AT PENKETH. A SCROOLPELLOWR RENILVISCENCES. AN INTERESTING LETTER.

With reference to the late Mr. Bright's school- days at Periketn, which were refeired to in the last issue of '• The Examiner," Mr. Peter Davies, of Res-brook, co. Armagh, with whose father Mr. Bright lodged, and who was a schoolmate of the deceased statesman, sends the following interesting particulars, together with an hitherto unpublished, atm very characteristic, letter written by Mr. Bright . _ .

• • . • .3-mght years have gone by, says Mr. Davies," , "since John Bright and I were schoolfellows and lie.!- fellows at Periket but, notwithstanding, my recol- lection of him as I knew him at that time is clear and distinct. That in any account of John Brigitte early life that I have ever seen no allusion should have been made to the time he spent at Penketh has often seemed to me remarkable, and probably it is not at all generally knawn that he was at school there. It was, I believe,in 1822 that he went to Penketh. Ills health then was not very robust. and no doubt it was on that account that it was arranged with my father that he should reside with us, in order that he might have some of the atten- tions and comforts of home. The school was not a boarding school, and the present Penketh Friends' School was not established until some years after- wards. The school which we attended (John Bright, my only brother, and myself) was held in a large upper room of a house on the Common, close by the Meeting House, and about a quarter of a mile from my father's residence ; and the approach to the schoolroom was by a Hight of stone steps at , the outside of one of the gables. The old red brick farmhouse in which I was born (and some of my children al.) is little changed, save that the fruit trees that were trained over a good part of it have; been cut down. But the surroundinga ; alas! llow different from what they were in my boyhood ! The large old-fashioned garden, with its beehives and famous for the variety and abundance of the fruit which it produced, retains none of its former luxuriance -so I am told by one of my sons who visited the old place not long ago. The cause of this. I suppose, is to be laid at the leer of the neighbouring chemical works. The large range of farm buildings erected by my father is now converted into cottages. In old times it was a pleasant place. The grass and the hedgerows were green, and the flowers flourished and bloomed in profusion. It is this home of my boyhood with which my early recollections of john Bright are associated. I have said that he went to l'enketh in 1322, and if my memory serve me, he remained about eigh- teen months. The principal of the scholl was Joseph Edmondson: who was renowned amongst Friends for his erudition and for has singular abili- ties as a teacher, and I believe John Bright always entertained for him a high regard. Of boyish squab- bles and disagreements I do not remember any; in- deed, his disposition wa, quiet and exceedingly !amiable and unassuming, and he was a general favourite, not only with those of my father's house, but with the pupils at Joseph Edmondson's school. ' Though fond of his books and attentive to his les- sons, he took great interest and delight in out-door games and recreations. In resenting an injury, I think I never knew him to do so in any spirit of vindictiveness. On one occasion, when inn tnoment of irritation a teacher threw a Latin grammar at his head. John quietly picked up the hook and handed it back to him with the remark—, Thou migtat want this again." • •

A good deal of our spa, time was taken up in fishing, of which I have sometimes thought, when, in after life, I have read in the newspapers of his angling excursions in Scotland ; and during a vaca- tion my brother and I spent with him at his home, Itching, I remember, was our chief out-door amuse- ment. _

—ln reply to some words of congratulation which I sent him on his seventieth birthday, I received a let- ter which contains some allusion to the time he spent at Penketh. I give a copy or the letter, and have no doubt that it vastly exceeds in interest anything I have written "One Ash, Rochdale, Nov. 20,1881. My dear Friend, . .

Thy letter has given me much pleasure. It is long since we lived in the same house—the farm house at Penketh--but I like to look back to the pleasant time which I spent there. I remember the kindness of thy father, and of all his household, and have often of Into years intended to make a pilgrimage to the scenes of my school days, now sixty years ago, but occupation has kept me away. The Irish question is not yet quite settled, though we have done our best in order to settle it, but time and patience are needed, and we moot wait and hope. I should like to have a " talk "so Irish land and farmers, and prospects, and how you get on in the County Armagh better than in the South, but even the North has not been free from difficulty. I hope now the friends of onler will be able to speak out, and to help to repress the disorderly and barbarous proceedings which seem no common in some parts or the country. I am glad to have heard from an old school fellow and friend, though we have met so rarely during the sixty years which have passed since we were at school together. I am thy sincere friend
JOIN BRIGHT.
To Peter Davies Bembrook. County Armagh.
